claims.text: As-produced HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure containing multiscale chemical fluctuations and interfaces.
In situ imaging and digital image correlation will monitor local crack initiation and propagation during tensile and fracture experiments.
A reduced-order machine-learning model can capture local stress-strain fields in real time from concurrent microstructural and deformation data.
Grain-scale composition variations and interface networks govern evolving local stress states, dislocation activity, and crack propagation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Coupling live measurements of strain localization and crack growth to a surrogate model enables rapid refinement of its predictions.
The proposed coupling aligns measured local mechanical responses with global Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
The integrated framework will predict Young's modulus for HfNbTiVAl10.
The integrated framework will predict yield strength for HfNbTiVAl10.
The integrated framework will predict toughness for HfNbTiVAl10.
The framework will be at least 20% more accurate than prior computationally intensive methods.
The framework will reduce computation time by an order of magnitude.
Ab initio and molecular-dynamics methods are time-consuming, and CALPHAD can require significant computing resources.
Existing CALPHAD, first-principles, and machine-learning models predict strength and elastic properties with 70–80% accuracy.
Existing models have poor fidelity for fracture-property prediction.
The proposed framework will remain applicable up to approximately 800°C under quasi-static to intermediate tensile and fracture loading.
Reliability may decrease for compositions or microstructures outside the model's calibration domain.
Unanticipated phase transformations outside the tested conditions may make the approach unreliable.
Prior demonstrations of fracture prediction in multiphase refractory alloys are limited.
The prospective benchmark will use blinded HfNbTiVAl10 specimens with compositional or processing variations within ±2 at.% per element.
The hypothesis will be rejected if prediction errors exceed 20% in at least half of the blind tests.
